presentingComplaint: Sudden collapse with left flank and back pain, initially triaged as renal colic
history: 76-year-old man, ex-smoker (50 pack-years), longstanding hypertension and known COPD, brought in after a witnessed syncopal episode at home. Two hours earlier he developed abrupt, severe left flank and lumbar back pain radiating to the left groin, with one episode of vomiting. The junior triage note labelled this 'likely renal colic' because of the flank-to-groin radiation and prior nephrolithiasis. However the pain is constant (not colicky), unrelieved by position, and was accompanied by transient loss of consciousness with pallor and sweating. No haematuria reported. He is on amlodipine and had not previously had aortic imaging. Over 40 minutes in the department he became progressively drowsy and clammy.
examination: Cold, pale, diaphoretic and restless. Peripheries poorly perfused with thready pulses. Abdomen shows a tender, expansile, pulsatile epigastric/periumbilical mass with left flank fullness and bruising developing over the left loin (early Grey-Turner). Peritonism in the left flank. Femoral pulses palpable but weak and symmetric. No focal neurology.

labs.bloodGroupCrossmatch: urgent 6 units packed cells requested (massive transfusion protocol activated)

imaging: Bedside FAST/aortic POCUS: dilated infrarenal aorta ~8.2 cm with surrounding hypoechoic retroperitoneal fluid. Emergent non-contrast then CT angiogram (haemodynamics briefly permitting): 8.3 cm infrarenal fusiform abdominal aortic aneurysm with a large left-sided retroperitoneal haematoma and active contrast extravasation — confirmed rupture.
microbiology: Not applicable (non-infective vascular catastrophe); blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Aortic dissection extending to abdominal aorta
finalDiagnosis: Ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (8.3 cm) with retroperitoneal haemorrhage and haemorrhagic shock
citations: European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) — Management of Abdominal Aorto-iliac Artery Aneurysms — 2019
Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) — Care of Patients with an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm — 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Diseases of the Aorta
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective diagnosis; no antibiotics indicated. This is a time-critical surgical emergency.
contraindications: Avoid aggressive crystalloid over-resuscitation — target permissive hypotension (systolic ~70-90 mmHg while conscious) to limit clot disruption
Do not delay for extensive imaging in the crashing patient — transfer directly to theatre
Avoid opioid-induced hypotension without volume/blood readiness
edgeCases: Flank-to-groin pain radiation misattributed to renal colic is a classic lethal pitfall in elderly hypertensive men
Femoral pulses may remain palpable and symmetric despite rupture, falsely reassuring against dissection
Contained retroperitoneal rupture can produce transient haemodynamic stabilisation before catastrophic free rupture
expectedMaiK: Recognise haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured AAA: activate vascular surgery and massive transfusion protocol immediately, apply permissive hypotension, and move to theatre/EVAR rather than pursuing a renal-colic workup.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there a known AAA or prior aortic imaging?
Is the abdominal mass pulsatile and expansile?
Character of pain — constant tearing vs colicky?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent CT angiogram of aorta if haemodynamically permissible
Group and crossmatch 6 units + activate massive transfusion protocol
Point-of-care haemoglobin, lactate, coagulation and renal function

investigations: Group and crossmatch + massive transfusion protocol

regressionAssertions: Model must prioritise ruptured AAA over the renal-colic triage label given pulsatile expansile mass + shock
Management must include permissive hypotension and immediate vascular surgery activation, not fluid overload
